title: Mirabel and the Interior
premise: Cyrus Montrose, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost her sense of taste years ago and hides it behind devastating prose, is assigned a profile of Mirabel Okonkwo, the last fluent speaker of a dying language. Mirabel agrees to teach her only if Cyrus becomes a true student, and through vocabulary lessons Cyrus begins to taste again—just as she uncovers that Mirabel's estranged family has been keeping a secret about the mother's death and the land they're selling beneath her. The question the family arranged itself around—who was loyal, and who told the truth—threatens to destroy them before the mother's memory fades entirely. In the end, Cyrus publishes nothing: instead she records Mirabel's final testimony in the language itself, testifies at the land hearing as a witness rather than a critic, and chooses the uncomfortable visibility of truth over the safety of her polished invisibility.
about_author: Paloma Ravensworth is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent a decade translating testimony in three languages before turning to fiction. She writes about people caught between what they are asked to say and what they know to be true.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. At an awards dinner, Cyrus delivers a glowing review of a meal she couldn't taste, then deflects a young chef's earnest questions with her signature smile. Her editor assigns her a human-interest profile of Mirabel Okonkwo. Beat: we see the cost of her perfected armor—competence without appetite.

chapters.title: A House Full of Half-Words
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. She arrives at the Okonkwo home for the first interview and is intercepted by Mirabel's son Emeka, who offers a rehearsed, flattering version of his mother's life. Mirabel watches from the doorway and says, in English, almost nothing. Beat: the family's careful architecture of silence becomes visible.

chapters.title: One Student
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel refuses the interview but offers a counterproposal: one final student, daily lessons, no notes published until she says so. Cyrus, professionally cornered and privately hungry, accepts. First lesson: the word for 'taste' and the word for 'duty' share a root. Beat: reluctant covenant formed.

chapters.title: Salt Returning
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Weeks of lessons; Cyrus tastes salt on her tongue for the first time in six years while learning the word for rain. She begins eating alone, secretly, like a relapse. Meanwhile she notices surveyors' stakes on the family's land. Beat: wonder shadowed by the first crack in the family story.

chapters.title: What Emeka Arranged
chapters.summary: Emeka's POV. Emeka, managing the sale of the land to cover their mother's care, has built the family's consensus around a version of events from the night their father died. His sister Adaeze challenges him; he smooths it over with duty and debt. Beat: love expressed as control; the reader sees his fear, not villainy.

chapters.title: The Question Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. During a lesson, Mirabel falters mid-sentence—a memory going—and asks Cyrus directly: do you want my language, or my truth? She reveals there was a witness to the father's death whose account was never recorded. Beat: the stakes shift from profile to inheritance of truth.

chapters.title: Adaeze Breaks Rank
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Adaeze, the daughter who left, returns and confronts Emeka with what she saw as a child: their mother lied to protect someone—or was made to. The family fractures over dinner; Mirabel, present but fading, cannot settle it. Beat: loyalty and truth pull the siblings apart in front of the guest.

chapters.title: Everything I Was Paid to Forget
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus discovers her editor plans to run the profile early, framed as a sentimental obituary-in-advance, and realizes her drafts contain enough to expose the family's secret publicly. Offered the choice—kill the piece or betray Mirabel—she burns her draft and resigns. Beat: climax of vocation; she loses the career built on invisibility.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. At the land hearing, with Mirabel's memory nearly gone, Cyrus stands as witness—not quoting the article she never wrote, but speaking the testimony Mirabel gave her in the dying language, translated line by line. Emeka must choose between objecting and listening; he listens. Beat: justice outside the law, delivered as translation.

chapters.title: Two Words Left
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, closing with Cyrus. Mirabel teaches Cyrus the last two words she retains—one meaning 'stay,' one meaning 'true'—and dies knowing the language now has one more speaker, however imperfect. Cyrus, unemployed and tasting everything, begins writing a book no editor assigned. Beat: grief braided with arrival; love chosen over duty, finally, by everyone.
